candidates.teaser: Your eye has a hole in it — and your brain has been lying to you about it your entire life.
candidates.video_title: Your Eye Has a Blind Spot and You Never Noticed
candidates.video_description: Every human eye has a spot with zero photoreceptors — a literal hole in your vision. Your brain quietly fills it in with fabricated imagery so you never notice. It's happening right now.
candidates.script: You have a hole in your vision right now and you have absolutely no idea. Every human eye has a spot on the retina where the optic nerve connects — and that spot has zero light receptors. Zero. Meaning part of what you see at this very moment is completely made up by your brain. It stitches together surrounding details and fills in the gap like a photo editing tool, all in real time, without asking you. This has been happening every waking second of your life. So here's the question — if your brain is willing to invent part of reality just to keep you calm, what else is it quietly making up?

candidates.topic: Cleopatra's time period closer to Moon landing than pyramids
candidates.teaser: The pyramids are so ancient that Cleopatra was closer to the Moon landing than to them — but that's not even the wildest timeline fact.
candidates.video_title: Mammoths Were Alive When the Pyramids Were Built
candidates.video_description: While Egyptians were constructing the Great Pyramid, woolly mammoths still roamed a small Arctic island. History's timeline is far stranger than any textbook suggests.
candidates.script: When the ancient Egyptians were laying the final stones of the Great Pyramid, woolly mammoths were still alive. Not fossils. Not myths. Living, breathing mammoths on a remote Arctic island called Wrangel Island, roughly 4,000 years ago. We tend to picture mammoths as prehistoric creatures from some unimaginably distant past — but they overlapped with one of humanity's greatest engineering achievements. The last mammoth died around 1650 BC. That means mammoths outlived the pyramid's construction by centuries. History doesn't move in a straight line the way we imagine it. So which other animals do you think were still around during moments that would completely shock you?

candidates.topic: Trees can count and tell time
candidates.teaser: Trees don't have brains — but somehow they can count days, remember seasons, and time events perfectly.
candidates.video_title: Trees Can Count — And Nobody Talks About It
candidates.video_description: Trees track time using internal chemical clocks, counting cold days to know when to bloom. This biological calendar is so precise that scientists use it to study climate change across centuries.
candidates.script: Trees have no brain, no nervous system, and no eyes — but they can count. Every winter, a tree chemically tracks how many cold days have passed. It's not guessing. It's running a biological calculation called vernalization, waiting for a precise threshold before it allows itself to bloom in spring. Bloom too early and a late frost kills the flowers. Too late and pollination windows are missed. The tree solves this problem flawlessly, every single year, using nothing but chemistry. Some trees even remember drought patterns from decades ago and adjust their behavior accordingly. If a tree with no brain can keep better track of time than most of us — what exactly does that say about us?

candidates.topic: Sound can kill or levitate objects
candidates.teaser: Sound is invisible — but under the right conditions it can lift objects, shatter organs, and even stop a heart.
candidates.video_title: Sound Can Actually Kill You — Here's How
candidates.video_description: Acoustic levitation is real — scientists use sound waves to suspend objects in mid-air. But at the other extreme, infrasound at the right frequency can cause fatal organ damage. Sound is more powerful than you think.
candidates.script: Sound can levitate objects. Scientists do it in labs right now — ultrasonic waves create pressure fields strong enough to suspend water droplets, insects, even small stones in mid-air with no contact at all. But sound has a darker side too. Infrasound — frequencies too low for humans to hear — can travel through walls, through your body, and at the right intensity, cause disorientation, nausea, and at extreme levels, rupture internal organs. Some researchers believe certain infrasound frequencies trigger the feeling of being watched, which might explain reported hauntings in old buildings with rumbling pipes. Sound is invisible, yet it can move matter and mess with your mind. Makes you wonder — what are you hearing right now that you can't actually hear?

candidates.topic: The sun's light takes 100,000 years to escape the core
candidates.teaser: The sunlight hitting your face right now started its journey before modern humans even existed.
candidates.video_title: Sunlight Took 100,000 Years to Reach Your Face
candidates.video_description: A photon of light takes only 8 minutes to travel from the sun's surface to Earth — but escaping the sun's core to reach the surface takes around 100,000 years. The light you feel today is ancient.
candidates.script: The sunlight warming your skin right now is ancient. A photon of light is born in the sun's core through nuclear fusion, and from that moment, it begins an impossible journey outward — but the core is so incredibly dense that the photon bounces in random directions for approximately 100,000 years before it finally escapes the surface. Then, once free, it crosses 150 million kilometers of empty space in just eight minutes and lands on your face. That means the light you felt on your way to work this morning was created around the time early humans were first developing language. The sun has been sending you messages from the Stone Age. So what message do you think today's light is carrying?
